commentary: Aquinas opens by explaining why this book turns to substance as the proper object of first philosophy. Everything else predicated of a thing—quality, quantity, relation, and the rest—exists only because a substance exists to bear it; strip away substance and nothing else remains standing. This is why the earlier natural philosophers, in searching for principles and causes, were in fact always searching for the principles of substances, even when they didn't say so. Aquinas then follows Aristotle in sorting substance into three kinds: sensible substances subject to generation and corruption (plants, animals, the ordinary things around us), sensible substances that are eternal though still bodily (the heavenly bodies, which move but do not come to be or perish), and a third kind that is wholly separate from matter and motion altogether. He is careful about the status of this third kind: earlier thinkers who posited it—those who spoke of separate Forms, or of mathematical objects existing on their own—disagreed about how many such immaterial realities there are and how they relate to sensible things. Aquinas notes that the first two kinds of substance fall under natural philosophy, since both involve motion in some way, while the immaterial kind, if it exists, requires a distinct science to study it—namely, the one this whole treatise pursues. His point is architectonic: the entire investigation of Book Twelve is set up as an ascent from the substances we know through the senses toward one that is not sensible at all, and this ascent is what justifies metaphysics as a science in its own right.

Turning to sensible substance, Aquinas walks through Aristotle's account of change as requiring three things: a subject that persists, and two contrary terms, one lost and one gained. Since the contraries themselves cannot survive the change (whiteness does not become blackness), something else must underlie both—this is matter, understood not as a third "thing" alongside form and privation but as the potency that can be informed first one way and then another. Aquinas stresses the technical point that grounds the whole chapter: everything that comes to be, comes to be from what is potentially but not yet actually what it becomes, not from sheer nothingness. This lets Aquinas credit the older physicists, notably Anaxagoras with his talk of an original "all things together," with having groped toward the notion of potency without ever formulating it properly—their mixture-doctrines are best read charitably as confused approaches to prime matter and potentiality. He also lingers on the puzzle of how something can come from "non-being," distinguishing the different senses of that phrase so that generation is not made to look like the production of being from absolute nothing, which would violate the principle that nothing comes from nothing without qualification. Aquinas closes by drawing the chapter's threefold conclusion: every changeable substance is analyzed by three principles—matter as the substrate, form (or the privation of form) as the term reached or lost. This threefold analysis becomes the tool Aquinas will use throughout the rest of the book to distinguish sensible substances from the immaterial substance still to come.

Here Aquinas addresses a subtlety that will matter greatly for his own theology later: neither ultimate matter nor substantial form, strictly speaking, "comes to be." What comes to be is always the composite—this bronze sphere, this man—not the bronze or the sphere-shape taken by themselves, since positing generation of the principles themselves would send the analysis into an infinite regress with no stopping point. Aquinas also develops Aristotle's rule that generation proceeds from an agent bearing the same specific form as the effect: a man is begotten by a man, not produced from an abstract universal "humanity." This becomes the springboard for a direct critique of Plato's separately subsisting Forms. If what actually causes a new individual to exist is always another concrete individual of the same kind, acting through its own form, there is no need to posit a separately existing Form of Man floating apart from particular men to explain why men generate men; the form already at work in the begetting parent does the job the Platonic Idea was invented for. Aquinas does allow one significant exception, which he flags for later development: some forms may persist after the composite dissolves, most notably the human intellective soul, since its characteristic operation, understanding, does not depend intrinsically on the body's matter in the way sensation does. He leaves it an open question whether the whole soul survives or only its intellectual part. The chapter overall establishes matter, privation, and form as adequate principles of sensible substance without recourse to separated universals.

Aquinas takes up the question of whether all things—substances, qualities, relations, quantities—share the very same principles, or only analogous ones. He rejects strict identity: an element cannot literally be shared across radically different categories, since an element must be simpler than and different from what it constitutes, and no single item could function as literally identical matter for both a substance and, say, a relation. Instead Aquinas explains Aristotle's more careful answer: causes are the same only "by analogy," not univocally. Within one genus, such as sensible bodies, things do share literally common principles (hot and cold as formal principles, an underlying subject as matter); but across radically different genera, the sameness is only proportional—as form, privation, and matter stand to color, so they stand, proportionally, to day and night, light and darkness and air serving as the analogous triad. Aquinas draws out the deeper lesson: besides the intrinsic principles (matter and form) constituting a thing, there is always also an extrinsic moving cause, something already actual that brings the change about, and this fourth item—the efficient cause—is what ties every particular chain of change back, ultimately, to something first. This chapter thus quietly sets up the entire argument of the book: analogical causal structure across all beings points toward a single ultimate mover standing behind the diversified causal orders, glimpsed here through the recurring figure of "that which first of all moves all things."

Building on the analogy of causes, Aquinas develops the pairing of act and potency as principles that cut across every category of being, more fundamental even than matter and form themselves. The same subject, such as wine or flesh, can be actually one thing and potentially another at different times; but Aquinas is careful to note a further complication—sometimes cause and effect do not share matter in the same way, as when a father generates a son (an external per se cause) while the sun's motion along the ecliptic also contributes causally to generation and corruption in the sublunary world, without being the son's matter or form at all. Aquinas draws special attention to the principle that universal causes, strictly speaking, do not exist as separate agents: it is always an individual that causes an individual—this man, not "man in general," begets that man, just as your particular father, not fatherhood as such, caused you. This is another quiet rebuttal of Platonism, denying that a separately subsisting universal could do a singular thing's causal work. At the same time Aquinas shows how, despite this radical individuality of efficient causation, one can still speak truly and universally about causes in the abstract, since matter, form, privation, and mover remain the same in kind across individuals of a species even though numerically different in each. The chapter closes his survey of sensible substance and its principles, preparing the transition to the immaterial substance argued for in what follows.

This is the chapter's pivotal argument, and Aquinas gives it careful attention. Because motion and time can neither have begun nor can they cease—there could be no "before" without time already presupposed—there must exist some substance capable of sustaining eternal motion. Aquinas insists this cause cannot be merely potential, a substance that merely could move things but might not; potency by itself explains nothing necessary, since what is merely potential need not ever be actualized. Hence there must be some principle whose very essence is actuality itself, with no unrealized potency in it at all—which is also why Aquinas concludes this substance must be immaterial, since matter is precisely the principle of potentiality. He addresses a natural objection: doesn't potency always precede act, since a thing must first be able to act before it does? Aquinas, following Aristotle, answers that while in any single changeable thing potency for a given act may temporally precede its exercise, actuality is absolutely and simply prior in the order of causality, since only something already actual can bring another thing from potency into act. Notably, Aquinas here reads Aristotle as a philosopher arguing strictly from natural reason about motion's past eternity, distinguishing this philosophical conclusion from the truth of creation in time, which Aquinas elsewhere holds as an article of Catholic faith not owed to natural demonstration. The chapter ends by affirming that a pure, eternally active first cause—rather than "chaos" or the mythical accounts of the poets—best explains why some things move in one fixed way, and others vary.

Having proved a first unmoved mover must exist, Aquinas now explains how it moves without itself being moved: it acts as an object of desire and understanding, not as a mechanical push. Ordinary movers act by contact and are themselves altered in acting; but the first mover causes motion the way something loved moves a lover, purely as a final cause, drawing the heavens' desire and intellect toward itself without undergoing any change in the process. Aquinas develops the identification of this substance's activity with pure intellection: since God's substance is not composite, his understanding and his being are one, and since only the noblest object is fit for the noblest act of understanding, God's thinking has no object but himself—thought thinking itself. Aquinas underscores that this self-contemplation is also, properly speaking, life in the fullest sense, since life consists in immanent activity, and intellectual activity is life's highest form; hence God is rightly called a living, eternal, and supremely good being. He then refutes Speusippus and the Pythagoreans, who held that perfection appears only at the end of a process (as fruit follows seed) rather than at the beginning. Aquinas insists this gets causality backward: whatever produces something must already actually possess, in a higher way, the perfection it communicates—the seed itself only exists because a prior complete organism produced it. The chapter closes by establishing that this first substance has no magnitude, being incapable of the finite power a body would entail, and is wholly impassible and unchangeable, since even alteration presupposes the more basic reality of spatial motion, which this substance transcends entirely.

Aquinas now asks whether one such immaterial substance suffices or whether many must be posited, and here his surviving commentary becomes especially rich before it is cut short. His reasoning: each distinct eternal circular motion observed in the heavens—not only that of the outermost sphere but each planet's proper motion—requires its own proportionate, eternal, unmoved cause, since an eternal effect needs an eternal cause suited to it. Since astronomy detects multiple independent celestial motions, there must be a corresponding plurality of separate immaterial substances, one for each. Aquinas patiently works through the specific models of Eudoxus and Callippus, tallying the concentric spheres each assigns to the sun, moon, and planets, to arrive at a working total for how many unmoved movers exist beyond the first—while candidly noting, as Aristotle himself does, that the precise number is a matter for astronomers to determine more exactly and remains provisional. As his exposition proceeds, Aquinas introduces later Arabic commentary into the discussion, weighing Avicenna's view on whether the outermost heaven is moved immediately by the first principle itself or rather by a subordinate intelligence caused by it—a distinction Aquinas elsewhere uses to relate Aristotle's plural unmoved movers to the angelic intelligences of Christian doctrine, without simply equating the two. It is in the middle of unpacking this very question, weighing how much plurality of causality such subordinate movers introduce, that the text of Aquinas's commentary breaks off, apparently mid-sentence, before the chapter's own argument for the unity of the physical universe and its concluding remarks on the ancient mythical tradition about the gods is ever reached.
